facts.claim: Danno Simpson's 'Honest Work' was released on November 6, 2020 by Pothole Records as the title track of a 5-track, roughly 18-minute EP.
The song 'Honest Work' is credited to Daniel Simpson (Danno Simpson) as composer and lyricist.
Jackson Earles plays fiddle on 'Honest Work'.
The EP 'Honest Work' was Simpson's self-produced debut EP, released in 2020.
BandWagon Magazine reports that 'Honest Work' was recorded in a cramped apartment bathroom and has more than a million Spotify plays.

Simpson recorded the EP of original Americana songs in his bathroom the year after his arrest and put it on streaming services during the height of the pandemic. 'Honest Work' then slowly gained streams from country fans.
A Jambands.com concert review says Simpson described 'Honest Work' as a 'hit piece' on an old boss.

Simpson was born in Texas, raised in Georgia, and now lives on Colorado's Front Range. His influences include Guy Clark, Townes Van Zandt and Steve Earle, and the mountain music of the Rockies and Appalachia.
Before his 2020 breakout, Simpson was part of the Fort Collins DIY punk scene. He says his punk-leaning songs were mistaken for country songs.
'Honest Work' is the biggest hit of Simpson's catalog to date. His later releases include the 2025 debut album 'The Kill Joy'.

research.lineage: Simpson's music sits in the Texas songwriter tradition (Townes Van Zandt, Guy Clark, Jerry Jeff Walker) and Appalachian and Rockies mountain music, within the growing Colorado alt-country/Americana scene that grew out of Fort Collins DIY punk.

draft:
A bathroom is a strange place to settle a score. **Honest Work** was cut in a cramped apartment bathroom, and the room comes through: a clean, close, natural space where a fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls out bright arpeggios and Danno Simpson sings right on top of them. The arrangement is spare, and guitar and voice carry it. It sounds like someone telling you a story across a small table.

By Simpson's own account onstage, the story is a "hit piece" on an old boss. That description is the key to the song's feeling, and to its quiet trick. A grudge usually wants volume. Simpson gives it a moderate tempo and an easygoing sway. His mid-range voice has a bit of rasp and gravel, and he delivers it like conversation, not accusation. The anger is in the premise, but the music keeps its temper. That gap is where the song lives: resentment told at a relaxed pace, the calm of someone who has replayed an old injury often enough that it has become a tale. The choice to tell it rather than yell it is what lets a listener lean in instead of backing away.

That calm has a backstory. Simpson came out of the Fort Collins DIY punk scene, where, he says, his punk-leaning songs kept getting mistaken for country. He wrote and self-produced the *Honest Work* EP, five original Americana songs running about 18 minutes. He recorded it the year after his arrest and put it on streaming services, through Pothole Records, during the height of the pandemic. The title track then caught on slowly, finding country listeners on its own and passing a million Spotify plays. It remains the biggest song in his catalog, ahead of later work like his 2025 debut album *The Kill Joy*.

The lineage he claims is the Texas songwriter line of Guy Clark, Townes Van Zandt and Steve Earle, alongside the mountain music of the Rockies and Appalachia. He was born in Texas, raised in Georgia, and now lives on Colorado's Front Range. You can hear why people took his songs for country. The fingerpicking and the plain storytelling voice sit squarely in that tradition. What carries over from punk is the target: this is a song with an enemy, and it doesn't pretend otherwise. Jackson Earles plays fiddle on it, a nod to the mountain side of that inheritance.

It sticks because it lets you sit with a grudge without being swallowed by it, and telling the story this calmly becomes its own small revenge.
